summary: This note describes reflex syncope, a brief loss of consciousness caused by a neurally induced drop in blood pressure and/or heart rate, divided into vasovagal, situational, and carotid sinus types. It covers warning signs, triggers, the underlying mechanism, diagnosis by ruling out other causes, and treatments including trigger avoidance, fluids and salt, medications, and occasionally pacemakers. The main danger is injury from falling while unconscious.
one_line: Overview of reflex syncope: its three types, warning signs, triggers, diagnosis, treatment options and prognosis.
key_facts: Reflex syncope is a brief loss of consciousness due to a neurologically induced drop in blood pressure and/or a decrease in heart rate.
Reflex syncope is divided into three types: vasovagal, situational, and carotid sinus.
Reflex syncope affects at least 1 in 1,000 people per year.
Reflex syncope is the most common type of syncope, making up more than 50% of all cases.
Vasovagal syncope is typically triggered by seeing blood, pain, emotional stress, or prolonged standing.
Situational syncope is often triggered by urination, swallowing, or coughing.
Carotid sinus syncope is due to pressure on the carotid sinus in the neck, which may happen when wearing a tight collar, shaving, or turning the head.
Before losing consciousness, a person may experience sweating, a decreased ability to see, or ringing in the ears.
In the vasovagal pathophysiology, the nucleus tractus solitarii of the brainstem is activated, enhancing parasympathetic tone and withdrawing sympathetic tone.
The vasodepressor end of the response spectrum can cause a blood pressure drop to as low as 80/20 without much change in heart rate.
The core of the diagnosis of vasovagal syncope rests upon a clear description of a typical pattern of triggers, symptoms, and time course.
Diagnostic tests for recurrent vasovagal syncope include a tilt table test, an insertable loop recorder, a Holter or event monitor, an echocardiogram, and an electrophysiology study.
The cornerstone of treatment is avoidance of triggers known to cause syncope in that person.
Beta blockers were once the most common medication given for vasovagal syncope but have been shown to be ineffective in a variety of studies and are no longer prescribed.
For people with the cardioinhibitory form of vasovagal syncope, implantation of a permanent pacemaker may be beneficial or even curative.
